passage: A structural biology group at the Okonkwo institute is purifying a recombinant enzyme that contains a single surface-exposed histidine near its active site. To locate the residue's ionization constant, the group titrated the protein in a series of buffers while following the histidine imidazole ring by NMR, which reports the fraction of side chains in the protonated, positively charged form. Protein concentration, ionic strength, and temperature were kept constant across buffers, and each measurement was repeated twice. The group later planned to bind the protein to a cation-exchange column and needed to understand how pH controls the protein's net charge. The protonation data also guided a decision about which buffering species to use for storage, since a buffer is most effective within about one pH unit of its own pKa. The protein was greater than 98% pure and monomeric by size-exclusion chromatography. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.
table:
Table 1. Protonation of the active-site histidine

| Buffer pH | Histidine side chains protonated (%) |
|---|---|
| 5 | 99 |
| 6 | 90.9 |
| 7 | 50 |
| 8 | 9.1 |
| 9 | 1 |

questions.stem: At which pH is the histidine approximately half-protonated?
questions.explanation: Half-protonation (about 50%) occurs at pH = pKa, which in Table 1 is pH 7.
questions.trap: Choosing pH 6 or pH 8 because they are near the midpoint, when about 50% protonated occurs exactly at pH = pKa.

questions.stem: Which design would best verify that the NMR signal reports histidine ionization and not a pH-dependent conformational change?

options.A: Repeat the titration with a variant in which the histidine is mutated to alanine
options.B: Repeat the titration at twice the protein concentration
options.C: Repeat the titration with a different counterion only
options.D: Repeat the titration without the protein

questions.explanation: Removing the titratable group should abolish the signal's pH dependence if it truly reports that residue.
questions.trap: Choosing a different protein concentration or counterion, which does not show whether the signal reports the histidine or a conformational change.

questions.stem: What is the ratio [protonated]:[deprotonated] at pH 6?
questions.explanation: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = −1 and [HA]/[A⁻] = 10^1 = 10.
questions.trap: Inverting the ratio to 1:10, or applying 100:1 when only one pH unit separates pH and pKa.

questions.stem: Which statement about buffers and this titration is INCORRECT?

options.A: A buffer's pH is independent of its conjugate base to acid ratio
options.B: The histidine side chain is mostly neutral at pH well above its pKa
options.C: Protonated histidine carries a positive charge
options.D: Buffering capacity is greatest near the pKa

questions.explanation: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation shows pH depends directly on the base-to-acid ratio.
questions.trap: Believing buffer pH is independent of the base-to-acid ratio, which contradicts the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.

questions.stem: At physiological pH, why do histidine residues frequently serve as general acid–base catalysts in enzymes?

options.A: Its side chain pKa is near physiological pH, so it can readily donate or accept a proton
options.B: Its side chain is always fully protonated at pH 7.4
options.C: Its side chain carries no ionizable group
options.D: Its side chain forms disulfide bonds with other residues

questions.explanation: A side chain pKa near 6–7 means both protonated and deprotonated forms are populated near pH 7.4, ideal for proton transfer in catalysis (e.g., serine proteases).
questions.trap: Believing histidine is fully protonated at physiological pH, when its pKa near neutrality means both forms are populated.
